desc:
A grid of letters is given as an integer matrix board (1 is a, ..., 26 is z). The grid wraps around: stepping off the right edge brings you to the left edge of the same row, stepping off the left edge brings you to the right edge, and the same holds between the top row and the bottom row.

Decide whether the lowercase string word can be spelled by a path that starts at any cell and moves one step at a time to the cell above, below, left or right (with wrapping). A cell may be used at most once in a path.

For example, on the single-row board [[1,2,3]] (the letters abc) the word cab can be spelled: after c the path steps right, wraps to a, and then reaches b. On the board with rows abc and def the word cfd can also be spelled, by going down from c to f and then right from f, wrapping to d.
hints: Start a search from every cell that holds the first letter, and extend letter by letter. The only change compared with an ordinary grid is how neighbours are computed.

Use modular arithmetic for the four neighbours: ((r - 1) % m, c), ((r + 1) % m, c), (r, (c - 1) % n), (r, (c + 1) % n). In a grid with 1 or 2 rows (or columns) some of these coincide with each other or with the cell itself, and the visited mark already forbids the cell itself, so it is enough to remove duplicates.

Mark the current cell as used before looking at the neighbours and unmark it afterwards. Cheap pruning: fail at once when the word has more copies of a letter than the board, or when it is longer than m * n; and begin from the end of the word that has the rarer letter on the board.
editorial: The search is the usual word-search backtracking: go(r, c, k) checks that the cell holds the k-th letter, finishes on the last letter, and otherwise tries the unused neighbours with letter k + 1. The wrap-around only changes the neighbour function, which now uses the remainder operator so every cell has four neighbours (fewer distinct ones when a dimension is 1 or 2).

Wrapping does not change the worst case, which is exponential in the word length, but the board has at most 25 cells and the letter-count check and the longer-than-the-board check remove the hopeless words. Reading the word backwards (when its last letter is rarer on the board) reduces the number of starting cells and is a valid trick because a path can be walked in either direction.
